practice.solution: **Q** is the general finding; **R** ('for instance') gives the first specific case, and **S**'s 'these memories' needs **R**. **P**'s 'therefore' concludes, and S6's 'this' refers back to it. **QRSP**.
practice.shortcut: General finding -> 'for instance' -> 'these memories' -> therefore.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** A new girl, Meena, joined our class in July. **P:** She had come from a village school that had just twenty students. **Q:** The two soon became inseparable friends. **R:** Our class teacher then asked Anu, the monitor, to help her settle in. **S:** Such a large class made her so nervous that she hardly spoke. **6.** Today Meena is one of the most popular students in school.
practice.solution: 'She' in **P** = Meena from S1. **S**'s 'Such a large class' contrasts with the twenty students in **P**, so the two form a pair. **R**'s 'then' is the teacher's response to her nervousness. **Q**'s 'The two' needs both Meena and Anu, so it follows **R**. **PSRQ**.
practice.shortcut: 'The two' needs both names; 'Such a large class' needs the twenty students.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Kalpana Chawla was born in Karnal, Haryana, in 1962. **P:** There she earned a doctorate and joined NASA. **Q:** In 1997, she became the first woman of Indian origin to fly into space. **R:** After studying aeronautical engineering in Chandigarh, she moved to the United States. **S:** Her second mission, in 2003, ended in tragedy when the shuttle Columbia broke up on its return. **6.** India still remembers her as a hero.
practice.solution: 'There' in **P** needs the country named in **R**, so they form a pair. Joining NASA comes before flying for it, so **P** is before **Q**. 'Her second mission' needs the first flight of 1997, so **Q** is before **S**. **RPQS**.
practice.shortcut: Place word 'There' pairs with the country; 'second mission' follows the first.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** One evening, an old traveller knocked at the door of a poor farmer. **P:** The next morning, the traveller left a small clay pot on the doorstep. **Q:** Inside the pot, the farmer found a bag of seeds and a note. **R:** The farmer shared his simple meal and gave the stranger a mat by the fire. **S:** He asked for some food and a place to rest for the night. **6.** The note said, 'Kindness, like these seeds, always grows.'
practice.solution: 'He' in **S** is the traveller from S1. **R**'s meal and mat answer **S**'s request. **P**'s 'The next morning' follows the night. **P** introduces 'a small clay pot', and **Q**'s 'Inside the pot' refers back to it, so **P****Q** is an a -> the pair. **SRPQ**.
practice.shortcut: a small clay pot -> the pot: the 'a' part comes first.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Last Sunday, my father brought home a second-hand bicycle. **P:** By evening, the bicycle looked almost new. **Q:** A mechanic nearby replaced the chain for fifty rupees. **R:** It came with a rusty chain and a torn seat. **S:** The seat was harder to fix, so my mother stitched a new cover for it. **6.** My sister took the first ride around the colony.
practice.solution: **R** introduces 'a rusty chain and a torn seat'. **Q**'s 'the chain' and **S**'s 'The seat' refer back to it. **S**'s 'harder' compares with the easy chain repair, so **Q****S** is a pair. **P**'s 'By evening' sums up the day's work. **RQSP**.
practice.shortcut: a chain / a seat -> the chain / the seat; 'harder' compares with the part before it.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Every monsoon, many Mumbai streets flood within hours. **P:** This problem gets worse when plastic waste blocks them. **Q:** The old drains of the city were built for far less rain. **R:** To tackle this, the city now cleans its main drains every May. **S:** This effort has reduced waterlogging at several spots. **6.** Experts, however, say the drains themselves must be rebuilt.
practice.solution: A chain of 'this' words: **P**'s 'This problem' = the undersized drains of **Q**; **R**'s 'To tackle this' = the blocked drains of **P**; **S**'s 'This effort' = the cleaning in **R**. **QPRS**.
practice.shortcut: this problem -> this -> this effort: each sums up the part before it.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Many young Indians are choosing to start their own businesses. **P:** These two factors have together created thousands of new businesses. **Q:** Cheap internet has made it possible to sell across the country from there. **R:** Government schemes also offer loans without security to first-time founders. **S:** This trend is strongest in small towns, not just in the big cities. **6.** Many of them now employ people from their own towns.
practice.solution: **S**'s 'This trend' is S1's trend, so it comes first. **Q**'s 'from there' = the small towns in **S**. **R**'s 'also' makes it a second factor, so it follows **Q**. **P**'s 'These two factors' needs both **Q** and **R**, so it is last. **SQRP**.
practice.shortcut: 'These two factors' can only come after both factors; 'also' marks the second.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Smartphones have put a camera in almost every pocket. **P:** People now take hundreds of photographs on a single trip. **Q:** Yet very few of these pictures are ever looked at again. **R:** Printing a few favourite photos, therefore, may be the best way to keep memories alive. **S:** Most stay buried in the phone until it is full or lost. **6.** An album on the shelf is still opened far more often than a phone gallery.
practice.solution: **Q**'s 'Yet ... these pictures' contradicts the huge number in **P**, so they form a contrast pair. **S**'s 'Most' continues from the pictures that are never seen again. **R**'s 'therefore' concludes. **PQSR**.
practice.shortcut: Yet + these pictures follows the claim it contradicts.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Antibiotics have saved millions of lives since the 1940s. **P:** Such resistant infections kill more than a million people worldwide every year. **Q:** The bacteria that survive then multiply and become resistant. **R:** But their careless use is now making them less effective. **S:** Many patients stop the course as soon as they feel better. **6.** Doctors therefore urge patients to finish every course they begin.
practice.solution: **R**'s 'But their careless use' contrasts with S1's claim that antibiotics save lives, so it follows S1 directly. **S** is an example of careless use. **Q**'s 'The bacteria that survive' are those left when the course is stopped early. **P**'s 'Such resistant infections' needs **Q**. **RSQP**.
practice.shortcut: The 'But' part answers S1 here; then example -> surviving bacteria -> such infections.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** India's Mars Orbiter Mission is remembered as a triumph of low-cost engineering. **P:** It was launched from Sriharikota in November 2013. **Q:** The orbiter kept sending pictures for nearly eight years, until contact was lost in 2022. **R:** India thus became the first country to reach Mars on its very first attempt. **S:** Ten months later, in September 2014, it entered orbit around Mars. **6.** Not bad for a mission that was planned to last just six months.
practice.solution: The dates run 2013 -> 2014 -> 2022. 'Ten months later' in **S** needs the launch in **P**. 'thus' in **R** draws the result of reaching orbit, so it follows **S**. S6's 'a mission planned to last just six months' comments on **Q**'s eight years, so **Q** is last. **PSRQ**.
practice.shortcut: Dates in order; 'Ten months later' anchors to the launch; 'thus' follows success.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** At half-time, our school football team was trailing 0-2 in the district final. **P:** Within ten minutes of the restart, our captain headed in a corner. **Q:** The winning goal came in the very last minute of the match. **R:** Twenty minutes later, our youngest player levelled the score at 2-2. **S:** In the dressing room, the coach told us to stop panicking and pass the ball more. **6.** By the final whistle, the whole school was on the field celebrating.
practice.solution: Half-time talk **S** comes before 'the restart' in **P**. 'Twenty minutes later' in **R** counts from **P**'s goal (1-2 -> 2-2). The winner **Q** comes last in the match. **SPRQ**.
practice.shortcut: Relative markers need an anchor: restart after the dressing room, 'twenty minutes later' after the first goal.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Heavy snow began falling on the Srinagar-Leh highway on Tuesday afternoon. **P:** Army teams reached the stranded travellers that evening with blankets and hot food. **Q:** Within hours, hundreds of trucks and cars were stuck near Zojila pass. **R:** Later that day, the vehicles were escorted slowly down to Sonamarg. **S:** By Wednesday morning, snowploughs had cleared a single lane. **6.** The highway was fully reopened only after a week.
practice.solution: Tuesday afternoon (S1) -> within hours **Q** -> that evening **P** -> 'By Wednesday morning' **S**, which sums up the night's clearing -> 'Later that day' **R**, which needs Wednesday. **QPSR**.
practice.shortcut: The by-phrase sums up the night's work; 'Later that day' anchors to Wednesday.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The school's annual day was to begin at 6 p.m. **P:** By the time the lights came back on, the audience had been waiting for over an hour. **Q:** For the next forty minutes, teachers searched the neighbourhood for a generator. **R:** By 5 o'clock, the hall was full of parents. **S:** At 5.30, just as the lights were being tested, the power went off. **6.** The children, however, performed so well that nobody complained.
practice.solution: The clock runs 5.00 **R** -> 5.30 **S**. 'For the next forty minutes' in **Q** counts from the power cut in **S**. **P**'s by-phrase sums up the whole wait — from 5 o'clock to after 6 — so it comes after the search. **RSQP**.
practice.shortcut: Two by-phrases: the first sets the scene, the second sums up the wait and comes last.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** When Meera reached the examination hall, the doors had already closed. **P:** She had then run the last two kilometres in the rain. **Q:** She had waited twenty minutes for another one before giving up. **R:** Seeing her soaked and breathless, the invigilator let her in with a warning. **S:** Her bus had broken down halfway to the city. **6.** She finished the paper with five minutes to spare.
practice.solution: S1 sets the scene in the simple past. **S**, **Q** and **P** are a past-perfect flashback explaining why she was late: breakdown -> 'another one' (bus) -> 'then' ran. **R** returns to the simple past and the main story, and S6 follows it. **SQPR**.
practice.shortcut: Past-perfect parts form the flashback; the simple-past part resumes the story.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The old lighthouse at the end of our beach no longer shines. **P:** A British engineer had built it in 1890 to guard ships from the rocks. **Q:** Then, in 2005, satellite navigation made the light unnecessary. **R:** Today, it serves as a small museum for tourists. **S:** For over a century, its keepers had lit the lamp every evening. **6.** Visitors can climb its 120 steps for a view of the whole coast.
practice.solution: Tense acts as a clock. 'had built' **P** is the earliest event, and 'had lit' for a century **S** follows the building. 'Then, in 2005' **Q** ends that period. The present tense in **R** ('Today') is last. **PSQR**.
practice.shortcut: Past perfect -> simple past -> present: the tenses run in the order of the events.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Making a cup of masala tea is simple. **P:** Once the water turns dark brown, pour in the milk and sugar. **Q:** Next, add the tea leaves and let them simmer for two minutes. **R:** First, boil water with crushed ginger and cardamom. **S:** Finally, strain the tea into cups. **6.** Serve it hot with biscuits.
practice.solution: 'First' **R** and 'Finally' **S** fix the ends. **P**'s 'Once the water turns dark brown' needs the tea leaves from **Q**. **RQPS**.
practice.shortcut: First/Finally fix the ends; the colour change needs the tea leaves.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Opening a savings account online now takes about fifteen minutes. **P:** Once the documents are checked, a short video call with a bank officer completes the process. **Q:** First, the applicant downloads the bank's app and enters her mobile number. **R:** She then uploads photos of her PAN card and Aadhaar card. **S:** An OTP sent to that number confirms her identity. **6.** The account number arrives by SMS the same day.
practice.solution: 'First' **Q** opens, and **S**'s 'that number' needs the number entered in **Q**. **P**'s 'the documents' are the cards uploaded in **R**, so **R****P** is a pair. Each step needs the one before it. **QSRP**.
practice.shortcut: Step dependencies: number -> OTP; upload -> documents checked.

practice.q:
Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a meaningful paragraph.

**P:** It is also the only mangrove forest that is home to tigers. **Q:** Rising sea levels, however, are now swallowing the islands they depend on. **R:** The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world. **S:** These tigers have learnt to swim between the islands.
practice.solution: Only **R** needs nothing before it — it names the Sundarbans. **P**'s 'It is also' refers to it, **S**'s 'These tigers' refers to **P**, and **Q**'s 'they' and 'the islands' refer to **S**. **RPSQ**.
practice.shortcut: No fixed ends: the one independent sentence opens, then follow the pointers.

practice.q:
Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a meaningful paragraph.

**P:** Children attend storytelling sessions there on weekends. **Q:** Libraries were once places only for silent reading. **R:** Adults, too, use their free computers to apply for jobs. **S:** Many have now become busy community centres.
practice.solution: **Q** is the only independent sentence. **S**'s 'Many' refers to the libraries and 'now' contrasts with 'once'. **P**'s 'there' needs the centres. **R**'s 'too' adds a second group, so it follows the children. **QSPR**.
practice.shortcut: Independent sentence first; 'too' marks the second of two examples.

practice.q:
Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a meaningful paragraph.

**P:** Yet many navy officers are still trained to read the stars in case the satellite signal fails. **Q:** Today, satellites tell a ship its exact position to within a few metres. **R:** The compass, which came later, made this far easier. **S:** For centuries, sailors used the stars to find their way at sea.
practice.solution: **R**'s 'this' is the navigation described in **S**, and 'which came later' places the compass after the stars. 'Today' in **Q** comes after both older methods. **P**'s 'Yet' and 'the satellite signal' need **Q**, so it ends the paragraph — the date-like 'Today' is not the ending here. **SRQP**.
practice.shortcut: Older -> later -> Today -> Yet: the contrast part closes.

practice.q:
Sentences P, Q, R and S, when properly arranged, form a meaningful paragraph. Which sentence should come FIRST?

**P:** He was carrying a small bag and looked lost. **Q:** A young boy got off the bus at the village stop one evening. **R:** The shopkeeper nearby asked him whom he was looking for. **S:** The boy replied that he had come to find his grandfather.
practice.solution: Orphan test: 'He', 'asked him' and 'The boy replied' all point back to someone already introduced. Only **Q** introduces 'A young boy', so it is first. Full order: **QPRS**.
practice.shortcut: The sentence with 'a' + new noun passes the orphan test.

practice.q:
Sentences P, Q, R and S, when properly arranged, form a meaningful paragraph. Which sentence should come FIRST?

**P:** Its roots grow down from the branches and look like extra trunks. **Q:** Over time, these hanging roots can spread a single tree over several acres. **R:** The banyan is India's national tree. **S:** The Great Banyan near Kolkata, for example, looks like a small forest from a distance.
practice.solution: 'Its roots', 'these hanging roots' and 'for example' all depend on an earlier sentence. **R** names the banyan and needs nothing before it, so it comes first. Full order: **RPQS**.
practice.shortcut: Pointers (Its, these, for example) rule out three sentences.

practice.q:
Sentences P, Q, R and S, when properly arranged, form a meaningful paragraph. Which sentence should come FIRST?

**P:** Kerala's boat races, similarly, draw crowds of thousands every August. **Q:** Festivals in India are often tied to rivers and the sea. **R:** In Bengal, for instance, Durga idols are immersed in the river at the end of the festival. **S:** Boats with over a hundred rowers race to the beat of songs.
practice.solution: Two sentences look independent: the general claim **Q** and the Kerala sentence **P**. But **P** contains 'similarly', so it needs an earlier example, and the Bengal sentence's 'for instance' needs the general claim before it. The general sentence **Q** is first. Full order: **QRPS**.
practice.shortcut: When two sentences look independent, check for hidden pointers (similarly) — the general claim wins.

practice.q:
Sentences P, Q, R and S, when properly arranged, form a meaningful paragraph. Which sentence should come LAST?

**P:** He buried it in a hole beside his garden wall. **Q:** A miser once sold everything he owned and bought a lump of gold. **R:** Every night he dug it up just to look at it. **S:** One day a thief, who had been watching him, stole the gold.
practice.solution: The story runs buy -> bury -> dig up nightly -> theft. **S**'s thief 'had been watching him' dig, so it comes after the nightly digging, and no sentence points back to the theft. **S** is last. Full order: **QPRS**.
practice.shortcut: The sentence that points back to all the others and is pointed to by none is last.

practice.q:
Sentences P, Q, R and S, when properly arranged, form a meaningful paragraph. Which sentence should come LAST?

**P:** Clearly, the key to saving water lies in fixing these small leaks at home. **Q:** Yet a surprising amount of water is lost inside our own homes. **R:** Most of us blame factories and farms for India's water crisis. **S:** A single dripping tap, for example, can waste thousands of litres a year.
practice.solution: **P** begins with 'Clearly' and its 'these small leaks' needs the dripping tap in **S**, so it sums up the paragraph and is last. Full order: **RQSP**.
practice.shortcut: Conclusion signal + 'these' pointer = the last sentence.

practice.q:
Sentences P, Q, R and S, when properly arranged, form a meaningful paragraph. Which sentence should come LAST?

**P:** 'Then you have already taken the first step,' replied the teacher. **Q:** The teacher asked him in turn, 'Do you know that you know very little?' **R:** The student admitted that he knew almost nothing. **S:** A student once asked his teacher how he could become wise.
practice.solution: The dialogue runs question **S** -> counter-question **Q** -> admission **R** -> reply **P**. The admission sounds like an ending, but the teacher's 'Then you have already taken the first step' answers it, so the reply **P** is last. Full order: **SQRP**.
practice.shortcut: In a dialogue, the last line answers the one before it — do not stop at the first line that sounds final.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** UPI has changed the way Indians pay for everyday things. **P:** But it has also made people spend more freely than before. **Q:** Even a roadside vegetable seller now displays a QR code. **R:** This has reduced the need to carry cash or look for change. **S:** Customers simply scan it and pay in seconds. **6.** Many now check their bank balance only at the end of the month.
practice.solution: **S**'s 'it' is the QR code in **Q**, and **R**'s 'This' is paying by scanning. If you are left with two strings that differ only in the order of **R** and **P**, test that link: 'But it has also' needs a benefit before it, so **R** comes before **P**. **QSRP**.
practice.shortcut: When two strings survive, test only the swapped pair: 'But ... also' follows the benefit.

practice.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The city decided to turn an old rubbish dump into a park. **P:** Workers first covered the heap with thick layers of clay and soil. **Q:** Birds that had not been seen in the area for decades began to return. **R:** Within three years, the saplings had grown into a small forest. **S:** On this new surface they planted grass and hundreds of saplings. **6.** The park now draws walkers every morning.
practice.solution: 'this new surface' in **S** is the soil layer of **P**. 'the saplings' in **R** were planted in **S**. The birds in **Q** return to the forest, so **Q** follows **R**. The nearest wrong strings swap two neighbouring parts; each swap breaks one of these pointers. **PSRQ**.
practice.shortcut: Check the one link that the surviving strings disagree on.

practice.q:
Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a meaningful paragraph.

**P:** Their numbers, however, have been falling sharply in many countries. **Q:** Pesticides and the loss of wild flowers are the main reasons for this decline. **R:** Farmers who plant flowering hedges around their fields are helping to reverse it. **S:** Honeybees and other pollinators help produce about a third of the food we eat.
practice.solution: **S** is the only independent sentence. 'Their numbers' in **P** refers to the pollinators, 'this decline' in **Q** is the falling numbers, and 'reverse it' in **R** needs the decline. **SPQR**.
practice.shortcut: Independent sentence, then Their -> this decline -> it.
